Islamic Movements: Are Programmes Expanding While Self-Purification Lags Behind?

The effective, credible, and sustainable development of an Islamic movement requires more than political activism alone. It equally depends on the continuous practice of self-purification (*Tazkiyat al-Nafs*).

**A personal observation:**

Visible organisational and political activities within Islamic circles are expanding day by day. Large public gatherings, extensive organisational growth, meetings, rallies, demonstrations, and public visibility are all increasing steadily.

However, it is not equally evident that this external expansion is being accompanied everywhere by a comparable growth in spiritual purification, character development, and moral excellence.

As a result, although outward activities may be increasing in many cases, it is difficult to say that the inner refinement, character formation, and practice of moral self-discipline among the movement’s leaders and activists are deepening at the same rate.

Yet, in Islamic thought, the reformation of the individual is the primary foundation of social reform. The Qur’an, too, establishes a profound connection between inner transformation and social change.

In other words, society changes when individuals change, and lasting reform in the external world becomes possible when the inner self is purified.

The greater the emphasis a movement places on purifying the inner self, the more likely it is to sustain its ideological commitment, moral credibility, and social influence over the long term.

For this reason, alongside organisational competence, political wisdom, and strategic capability, *Tazkiyat al-Nafs* should be regarded as a fundamental and inseparable component of Islamic politics.

Accordingly, in the daily life of a Muslim, voluntary prayers and fasting, in addition to obligatory acts of worship; regular recitation of the Qur’an accompanied by deep reflection; *dhikr* (remembrance of Allah); supplication; *istighfar* (seeking Allah’s forgiveness); *tawbah* (repentance); *Muhasabat al-Nafs* (self-examination); and the continuous struggle against the lower self and its desires (*Mujahadat al-Nafs*) should all form integral parts of a consciously cultivated way of life.

Self-purification is not merely a matter of personal piety or preparation for salvation in the Hereafter. It is also a fundamental basis for ethical leadership, restraint in the exercise of power, accountability, a sense of responsibility, and a political culture oriented towards public welfare.

History bears witness to the fact that movements which possess not only organisational strength but also a firm moral and spiritual foundation are better able to maintain a lasting balance between ideals, character, and public trust.

Conversely, when the practice of self-purification weakens, organisational strength and political success may themselves become vulnerable to the erosion of their moral foundations.

It is important to remember that political success is not the ultimate objective of an Islamic movement. Rather, politics is an important means in the broader endeavour to attain the pleasure of Allah, achieve moral excellence, and establish a society founded on justice.

To ensure that this means remains on the right course, self-purification is not optional. It is one of the principal foundations of an Islamic movement’s vitality, moral integrity, and long-term success.
